Gleb picked positive integers $N$ and $a$ ($a<N$). He wrote the number $a$ on a blackboard. Then at each turn he did the following: he took the last number on the blackboard, divided the number $N$ by this last number with remainder and wrote the remainder on the board. When he wrote the number $0$ on the board, he stopped. Could he pick $N$ and $a$ such that the sum of the numbers on the blackboard would become greater than $100N$?

Alice wrote a sequence of $n>2$ non-zero distinct numbers such that each is greater than the previous one by the same amount. Bob wrote the inverses of those $n$ numbers in some order. It so happened that each number in his row is also greater than the previous one by the same amount, possibly not the same as in Alice's sequence. What are the possible values of $n$?

On the table there are all $8$ possible horizontal $1\times 3$ bars such that each $1\times 1$ square is either white or grey (see the figure). It is allowed to move them in any direction by any (not necessarily integer) distance. We may not rotate them or turn them over. Is it possible to move the bars so that they do not overlap, all the white points form a polygon bounded by a closed non-self-intersecting broken line, and the same is true for all the grey points?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/totj_2021_d1_p2_fig.png

The hypotenuse of a right triangle has length $1$. Consider the line passing through the points of tangency of the incircle with the legs of the triangle. The circumcircle of the triangle cuts out a segment of this line. What can the length of this segment be?

The number $7$ is written on a board. Alice and Bob in turn (Alice begins) write an additional digit in the number on the board: it is allowed to write the digit at the beginning (provided the digit is non-zero), between any two digits, or at the end. If after someone's turn the number on the board is a perfect square, then this person wins. Is it possible for one of the players to guarantee a win?

A parallelogram $ABCD$ is split by the diagonal $BD$ into two equal triangles. A regular hexagon is inscribed in the triangle $ABD$ so that two of its consecutive sides lie on $AB$ and $AD$ and one of its vertices lies on $BD$. Another regular hexagon is inscribed in the triangle $CBD$ so that two of its consecutive vertices lie on $CB$ and $CD$ and one of its sides lies on $BD$. Which of the hexagons is bigger?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/totj_2021_d1_p5_fig.png

Let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denote the integer part of the number $x$, that is, the largest integer that is not greater than $x$. Prove that for any positive integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ the following inequality holds:
$$\left\lfloor\frac{a_1^2}{a_2}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{a_2^2}{a_3}\right\rfloor+\ldots+\left\lfloor\frac{a_n^2}{a_1}\right\rfloor\ge a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n.$$

There are $20$ buns with jam and $20$ buns with treacle arranged in a row in random order. Alice and Bob take in turn a bun from either end of the row. Alice starts, and wants to obtain in the end $10$ buns of each type; Bob tries to prevent this. Is it true that for any order of the buns Alice can win no matter what Bob does?
The number $2021=43\cdot 47$ is composite. Prove that if we insert any number of digits "8" between $20$ and $21$, then the number remains composite.

In a room there are several children and a pile of $1000$ sweets. The children come to the pile one after another in some order. Upon reaching the pile each of them divides the current number of sweets in the pile by the number of children in the room, rounds the result if it is not an integer, takes the resulting number of sweets from the pile and leaves the room. All the boys round upwards and all the girls round downwards. The process continues until everyone has left the room. Prove that the total number of sweets received by the boys does not depend on the order in which the children reach the pile.

There is an equilateral triangle $ABC$. Let $E$, $F$ and $K$ be points such that $E$ lies on the side $AB$, $F$ lies on the side $AC$, $K$ lies on the extension of the side $AB$, and $AE=CF=BK$. Let $P$ be the midpoint of the segment $EF$. Prove that the angle $KPC$ is right.

A traveller arrived at an island where $50$ natives lived. All the natives stood in a circle and each announced first the age of his left neighbour, then the age of his right neighbour. Each native is either a knight, who told both numbers correctly, or a knave, who increased one of the numbers by $1$ and decreased the other by $1$ (at his choice). Is it always possible after that to establish which of the natives are knights and which are knaves?

$100$ tourists arrive at a hotel at night. They know that in the hotel there are single rooms numbered $1, 2, \ldots, n$, and among them $k$ (the tourists do not know which) are under repair; the other rooms are free. The tourists, one after another, check the rooms in any order (maybe different for different tourists), and the first room not under repair is taken by the tourist. The tourists do not know whether a room is occupied until they check it. However, it is forbidden to check an occupied room, and the tourists may coordinate their strategy beforehand to avoid this situation. For each $k$ find the smallest $n$ for which the tourists can be sure to select their rooms.

Let $p$ and $q$ be two coprime positive integers. A frog hops along the integer line so that on every hop it moves either $p$ units to the right or $q$ units to the left. Eventually, the frog returns to the initial point. Prove that for every positive integer $d$ with $d<p+q$ there are two numbers visited by the frog which differ by exactly $d$.

One hundred friends, including Alice and Bob, live in several cities. Alice has found out the distance from her city to the city of each of the other $99$ friends and added up these $99$ numbers. Bob did the same thing as Alice. Alice got $1000$ km. What is the largest number that Bob could get? (Consider the cities as points in the plane; if two people live in the same city, the distance between their cities is considered to be zero.)

For the numbers $1, 19, 199, 1999$, etc., individual cards were made, one card for each number, with the corresponding number written on each card.
a) Is it possible to pick at least three cards so that the sum of the numbers on them equals a number in which all digits, except for a single digit, are twos?
b) Suppose you have picked several cards so that the sum of the numbers on them equals a number all of whose digits are twos except for a single digit. What can this digit be?
Baron Munchausen claims that he has drawn a polygon and a point inside it in such a way that any line passing through this point divides the polygon into three polygons. Could the Baron be right?

Let $n>1$ be an integer. A rook stands in one of the cells of an infinite white checkered board. With each move the rook shifts across the board by exactly $n$ cells, all vertically or all horizontally, painting the $n$ cells passed over black. After several moves in that manner, without visiting any cell twice, the rook returns to the starting cell. The black cells form a closed contour. Prove that the number of white cells inside this contour leaves a remainder of $1$ when divided by $n$.

On the sides of a regular nonagon $ABCDEFGHI$ the triangles $XAB$, $YBC$, $ZCD$ and $TDE$ are constructed outside the nonagon. The angles $X$, $Y$, $Z$, $T$ of these triangles are $20^\circ$ each. Among the angles $XAB$, $YBC$, $ZCD$ and $TDE$, each next angle is $20^\circ$ greater than the one listed before it. Prove that the points $X$, $Y$, $Z$, $T$ lie on one circle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/totj_2022_d1_p5_fig.png

Peter added a positive integer $M$ to a positive integer $N$ and noticed that the sum of the digits of the resulting integer is the same as the sum of the digits of $N$. Then he added $M$ to the result again, and so on. Will he necessarily get again a number with the same sum of digits as the number $N$?
Find the largest positive integer $n$ such that for each prime $p$ with $2<p<n$ the difference $n-p$ is also prime.

Prove that from any convex quadrilateral one can always cut out three smaller quadrilaterals similar to the original one with scale factor $1/2$. (The angles of a smaller quadrilateral are equal to the corresponding angles of the original one, and its sides are half as long as the corresponding sides of the original quadrilateral.)

For each of the nine positive integers $n, 2n, 3n, \ldots, 9n$ Alice takes the first decimal digit (from the left) and writes it on a blackboard. She selected $n$ so that among the nine digits on the blackboard there is the least possible number of different digits. What is this number of different digits?

Consider a white $100\times 100$ square. Several cells (not necessarily neighbouring) were painted black. In each row or column that contains some black cells, their number is odd. Hence we may consider the middle black cell of this row or column (with equal numbers of black cells in both opposite directions). It so happened that all the middle black cells of such rows lie in different columns and all the middle black cells of the columns lie in different rows.
a) Prove that there exists a cell that is both the middle black cell of its row and the middle black cell of its column.
b) Is it true that any middle black cell of a row is also the middle black cell of its column?

The intersection of two triangles is a hexagon. If this hexagon is removed, six small triangles remain. Those six triangles have the same radii of the incircles. Prove that the radii of the incircles of the two original triangles are also equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/totj_2022_d2_p5_fig.png

$7$ golden, $7$ silver and $7$ bronze medals were made for a tournament. All the medals of the same material should weigh the same, and medals of different materials should have different weights. However, it so happened that exactly one medal had a wrong weight. If this medal is golden, it is lighter than a standard golden medal; if it is bronze, it is heavier than a standard bronze one; if it is silver, it may be lighter or heavier than a standard silver one. Is it possible to find the non-standard medal for sure, using three weighings on a balance scale with no weights?

Let $p$ be a prime number and let $M$ be a convex polygon. Suppose that there are precisely $p$ ways to tile $M$ with equilateral triangles with side $1$ and squares with side $1$. Show that some side of $M$ has length $p-1$.

Every square of an $8\times 8$ board is filled with a positive integer such that the following condition holds: if a chess knight can move from some square to another, then the ratio of the numbers in these two squares is a prime number. Is it possible that some square is filled with $5$ and another one with $6$?
A unit square of paper has a triangle-shaped hole (the vertices of the hole are not on the border of the paper). Prove that a triangle of area $1/6$ can be cut from the remaining paper.

Let us call a $2\times 1$ two-square card regular if two positive integers are written on it and the number in the upper square is less than the number in the lower square. At each move it is allowed to change both numbers in one of the following ways: either add the same integer (possibly negative) to both numbers, or multiply each number by the same positive integer, or divide each number by the same positive integer. The card must remain regular after every change. What minimal number of moves is sufficient to get any regular card from any other regular card?

A triangle $ABC$ with angle $A$ equal to $60^\circ$ is given. Its incircle is tangent to the side $AB$ at the point $D$, while its excircle tangent to the side $AC$ is tangent to the extension of the side $AB$ at the point $E$. Prove that the perpendicular to the side $AC$ passing through the point $D$ meets the incircle again at a point equidistant from the points $E$ and $C$. (An excircle is a circle tangent to one side of the triangle and to the extensions of the two other sides.)

Tom has $13$ weights that look alike; $12$ of them weigh the same and the $13$th is fake and weighs more than the others. He also has two balances: one shows correctly which pan is heavier or that their weights are equal; the other gives the correct result when the weights on the pans differ, and gives a random result when the weights are equal. (Tom does not know which balance is which.) Tom can choose the balance before each weighing. Prove that he can surely determine the fake weight in three weighings.

A baker has baked a rectangular pancake. He then cut it into $n^2$ rectangles by making $n-1$ horizontal and $n-1$ vertical cuts. Rounded to the nearest integer, the areas of the resulting rectangles are equal to all the positive integers from $1$ to $n^2$ in some order. For which maximal $n$ could this happen? (Half-integers are rounded upwards.)

There are $100$ chess bishops on the white squares of a $100\times 100$ chessboard. Some of them are white and some of them are black. They can move in any order and capture bishops of the opposite colour. What number of moves is sufficient for sure to leave only one bishop on the chessboard?
A right-angled triangle has an angle equal to $30^\circ$. Prove that one of the bisectors of the triangle is half as long as another one.

There is a bacterium in one of the cells of a $10\times 10$ checkered board. At the first move the bacterium shifts to a cell adjacent by side to the original one and divides into two bacteria (both stay in the same cell). Then again one of the bacteria on the board shifts to a cell adjacent by side and divides into two bacteria, and so on. Is it possible that after some number of such moves the number of bacteria in each cell of the board is the same?

Let us call a positive integer pedestrian if all its decimal digits are equal to $0$ or $1$. Suppose that the product of some two pedestrian integers is also pedestrian. Is it necessarily true in this case that the sum of the digits of the product equals the product of the sums of the digits of the factors?

The sides of a regular triangle $ABC$ are also sides of triangles $AB'C$, $CA'B$, $BC'A$ constructed outside it. In the resulting hexagon $AB'CA'BC'$ each of the angles $A'BC'$, $C'AB'$, $B'CA'$ is greater than $120^\circ$, and the sides satisfy the equalities $AB'=AC'$, $BC'=BA'$, $CA'=CB'$. Prove that the segments $AB'$, $BC'$, $CA'$ can form a triangle.

The positive integers from $1$ to $100$ are painted in three colours: $50$ integers are red, $25$ integers are yellow and $25$ integers are green. The red and yellow integers can be divided into $25$ triples such that each triple includes two red integers and one yellow integer which is greater than one of the red integers and smaller than the other one. The similar assertion is valid for the red and green integers. Is it necessarily possible to divide all the $100$ integers into $25$ quadruples so that each quadruple includes two red integers, one yellow integer and one green integer such that the yellow and the green integers lie between the red ones?

Let $X$ be a set of integers which can be partitioned into $N$ disjoint increasing arithmetic progressions (infinite in both directions), and cannot be partitioned into a smaller number of such progressions. Is such a partition into $N$ progressions unique for every such $X$ if
a) $N=2$;
b) $N=3$?
(An increasing arithmetic progression is a sequence of numbers such that each number exceeds its left neighbour by the same quantity.)
A regular $100$-gon is dissected into some number of parallelograms and two triangles. Prove that these triangles are congruent.

Baron Munchausen took several cards and wrote a positive integer on each one (some numbers may be the same). The Baron reports that he has used only two distinct digits to do that. He also reports that among the leftmost digits of the sums of the integers on each pair of these cards there are all the digits from $1$ to $9$. Can it be that the Baron is right?

Peter and Basil take turns drawing roads in a plane, Peter starts. Each road is either a horizontal or a vertical line along which one can drive in only one direction (that direction is determined when the road is drawn). Can Basil always act in such a way that after each of his moves one could drive according to the rules between any two constructed crossroads, regardless of Peter's actions?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, its incentre $I$ and circumcentre $O$ are marked. The lines $AI$ and $CI$ meet the circumcircle of $ABC$ for the second time at the points $N$ and $M$ respectively. The segments $MN$ and $BO$ intersect at the point $X$. Prove that the lines $XI$ and $AC$ are perpendicular.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/totj_2024_d1_p3_fig.png

A triangle is constructed on each side of a convex polygon so that the third vertex of each triangle is the intersection point of the bisectors of the angles adjacent to this side. Prove that these triangles cover the whole polygon.

Let us call a move of a chess knight horizontal if it moves two cells horizontally and one vertically, and vertical otherwise. It is required to place the knight on a cell of a $46\times 46$ board and alternate horizontal and vertical moves. Prove that if each cell is visited at most once, then the number of moves does not exceed $2024$.

Two strictly increasing sequences of positive numbers are given. In each sequence, each number starting from the third one is the sum of the two preceding ones. It is known that each of the sequences contains at least one number not present in the other sequence. What is the maximum number of numbers common to these two sequences?

There were $12$ students at a physical education class, all of different strength. The coach divided them into two teams of $6$ students. He did so $10$ times, and each time the division was new. The teams played tug-of-war. Could it happen that all $10$ games resulted in a draw (i.e. the total strengths of the students in both teams were equal each time)?
Prove that among the vertices of any convex nonagon there are three vertices that form an obtuse triangle none of whose sides coincides with a side of the nonagon.

There is a pile of $100$ stones. There are two players. The first one picks $1$ stone, then the second one picks $1$ or $2$ stones, then the first one picks $1$, $2$ or $3$ stones, then the second one picks $1$, $2$, $3$ or $4$ stones, and so on. The one picking the last stone wins. Which player can ensure his victory regardless of the opponent's strategy?

Tom chose a positive irreducible fraction $x=\frac mn$. One can choose a positive fraction $y$ less than $1$, and Tom will tell the numerator of the irreducible fraction equal to the sum $x+y$. How can one determine $x$ for sure in two such actions?

There are $9$ vertical pillars standing in a row. There are horizontal sticks in some places between neighbouring pillars, no two of which are at the same height. A beetle crawls upwards, and whenever it reaches a stick, it crawls along it to the neighbouring pillar and carries on crawling upwards. It is known that if the beetle starts from the bottom of the first pillar, then it ends up at pillar nine. Is it always possible to remove one of the sticks so that the beetle would end up at the top of pillar five? (For instance, if the sticks are positioned as in the figure, then the beetle will follow the solid line. If the third stick on the beetle's way is removed, the beetle will crawl along the dotted line.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/totj_2024_d2_p5_fig.png

The points $M$ and $N$, $P$ and $Q$ are marked on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$; they are the midpoints of the arcs $BAC$, $CBA$, $BC$ and $AC$ respectively. The circle $\omega_1$ is tangent to the side $BC$ at the point $A_1$ and tangent to the extensions of the sides $AC$ and $AB$. The circle $\omega_2$ is tangent to the side $AC$ at the point $B_1$ and tangent to the extensions of the sides $BA$ and $BC$. It turned out that $A_1$ belongs to the segment $NP$. Prove that $B_1$ belongs to the segment $MQ$.

Distinct real numbers are printed on $99$ cards, one number on each card. Their total sum is irrational. A pile of the $99$ cards is called unfortunate if for every $k$ from $1$ to $99$ the sum of the numbers on the $k$ upper cards is irrational. Tom has calculated the number of all possible ways to put the cards into an unfortunate pile. What is the minimal number Tom could obtain?

In a $12$-digit number $A$, any two adjacent digits form a $2$-digit prime number, and all eleven of these primes are distinct.
a) What is the last digit of $A$?
b) Give an example of such a number $A$.

The angles $B$ and $C$ of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ are both equal to $120^\circ$. There is a point on the side $AD$ from which all the other sides are seen at the same angle. Find the angle between the diagonals of the quadrilateral.

a) Once upon a time, in a far away land there were $n$ cities but no roads between them. The hero started building roads one by one. Each time he selects the two closest cities not connected directly by a straight road and builds a straight road between them. His work ends when it becomes possible to go from any city to any other city (possibly with intermediate stops in other cities). Is it true that no two of the roads he builds intersect outside the cities?
b) The same question, but now each time the hero selects the two closest cities which are not connected by roads (even indirectly, with intermediate stops in other cities).
Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that there are exactly $1000$ squares strictly between $N^3$ and $(N+1)^3$.

A positive integer $k$ is given. Someone places $n$ coins of weights $1, 2, \ldots, n$ in a circle on the table; all the coins look identical. It is known that the weights go in increasing order, but we do not know the starting point and whether they increase clockwise or counterclockwise. You have a balance scale that allows you to take any two coins and find out which one is heavier (you can place only one coin on each side of the scale). Baron Munchausen claims that you can make at most $k$ such weighings and know for certain the weight of at least one coin. What is the largest $n$ for which this is true?

The teacher has chosen two different digits from $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 9\}$. Nick intends to find a seven-digit number divisible by $7$ whose decimal representation contains no digits other than these two. Is this possible for every choice of the teacher?

In a $2025\times 2025$ table, several cells are marked. In each move, Cyril can find out the number of marked cells in any square of cells inside the original table with side less than $2025$. What is the minimal number of moves that allows him to determine the total number of marked cells for sure?

In a triangle $ABC$ with right angle $C$, the altitude $CH$ is drawn. An arbitrary circle passing through the points $C$ and $H$ meets the segments $AC$, $CB$ and $BH$ for the second time at the points $Q$, $P$ and $R$ respectively. The segments $HP$ and $CR$ meet at the point $T$. Which is greater: the area of the triangle $CPT$ or the sum of the areas of the triangles $CQH$ and $HTR$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/totj_2025_d2_p3_fig.png

There are $15$ coins of the same appearance. It is known that one of them weighs $1$ g, two coins weigh $2$ g each, three coins weigh $3$ g each, four coins weigh $4$ g each, and five coins weigh $5$ g each. There are inscriptions on the coins indicating their weights. It is allowed to perform two weighings on a balance without additional weights. Find a way to check that there are no wrong inscriptions. (It is not required to find out which inscriptions are wrong and which ones are correct.)

A quadratic equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ with non-zero integer coefficients $a$, $b$ and $c$ is given, and it has an integer root. Can it happen that, whichever of these three coefficients is increased by $1$, the result is again a quadratic equation having an integer root?

There are $11$ watermelons of masses $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 11$ kg. Olya and Kolya put the watermelons into four bags; each bag holds $14$ kg and tears under a greater mass. In turn they choose any watermelon and put it into any of the bags so that the bag does not tear. The player who cannot make a move loses. Olya starts. Who can guarantee a win, no matter how the other plays?

On the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ with angle $B$ equal to $45^\circ$, points $Q$ and $P$ respectively are chosen so that the angle $BAP$ is three times smaller than the angle $A$, and the angle $BCQ$ is three times smaller than the angle $C$. Let $M$ be the intersection point of the segments $AP$ and $CQ$. The circumcircles of the triangles $BPM$ and $BQM$ meet the sides $AB$ and $BC$ for the second time at the points $N$ and $K$ respectively.
